cases.proof: Range-for over vector<int> of size n visits each of the n elements exactly once via begin()/end(), each with O(1) dereference and accumulation. No extra storage proportional to n is allocated.

Loop condition i < s.size() is checked n+1 times where n = s.size(); string::size() is O(1) and each iteration does O(1) work on s[i], so total time is O(n). Only scalar accumulator total is used, giving O(1) auxiliary space.
deque<int> iterators support O(1) increment/dereference; range-for visits all n elements exactly once, giving O(n) time and O(1) extra space beyond the accumulator.
The loop bound is the literal 100, not derived from any runtime input symbol. The function always performs exactly 100 additions regardless of caller data, which is constant work.
cases.assumptions: arr always has at least 100 valid elements (as declared by the parameter type int[100]).

cases.proof: Loop runs from 0 to n (exclusive) performing O(1) work per iteration (pointer indexing and addition), giving O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
cases.assumptions: arr points to a valid buffer of at least n elements, provided by the caller.

cases.proof: The outer range-for visits each row once and the inner range-for visits each element of that row once; summed across all rows this touches every element exactly once, so total time is O(N) where N is the total element count across all inner vectors. No storage grows with N.
cases.assumptions: N = sum of grid[i].size() over all i (total element count, not outer row count).

cases.proof: const-qualification does not change iteration cost: range-for over a const vector<long long>& still performs one O(1) step per element for all n elements.

vector<bool> is a bit-packed specialization, but its iterators still provide O(1) amortized access per element via proxy references. Visiting all n bits performs O(n) total work; only a scalar counter is kept, so space is O(1).

Manual iterator loop using v.begin()/v.end() is semantically identical to a range-for: each of the n elements is visited once with O(1) increment and dereference, giving O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
Outer loop runs n times; for each outer iteration the inner loop runs n times performing O(1) work, giving a total of n*n = O(n^2) operations. Only a scalar accumulator is used.
cases.assumptions: mat is an n x n matrix and n is the shared row/column dimension passed explicitly; no bounds checking is performed on mat's actual dimensions.

cases.proof: v.size() is called on every loop-condition check, but std::vector::size() is O(1), so re-evaluating it n+1 times contributes only O(n) total overhead, matching the O(n) cost of visiting each element once.
cases.assumptions: The vector is not mutated during the loop, so size() returns a stable value n across all checks.

cases.proof: Each iteration may push_back a new element whose presence depends on the runtime value v[i], and the loop bound v.size() grows as a result. The total number of iterations is a function of the actual data values (not just the initial size n) and cannot be bounded statically without knowing those values, so no fixed asymptotic bound can be assigned.
cases.assumptions: Bound depends entirely on runtime values in v; initial size is n but final iteration count is data-dependent and potentially unbounded if values are large or unbounded.

cases.proof: vector::erase(begin()) shifts all remaining elements left by one position, costing O(k) where k is the current size. Summing this cost over n iterations as the vector shrinks from n to 0 gives n + (n-1) + ... + 1 = O(n^2) total time. The function takes v by value, but no additional space proportional to n is allocated beyond that initial copy, so auxiliary space (beyond input) is O(1).
cases.assumptions: Auxiliary space excludes the by-value copy of the input vector itself, counting only extra space used by the algorithm's logic.

cases.proof: std::map is a balanced binary search tree; in-order iteration via range-for visits each of the n nodes exactly once with O(1) amortized successor cost per step, giving O(n) total time. Only a scalar accumulator is used beyond the input map.
cases.assumptions: n = m.size(); auxiliary space excludes the input map's own storage.

cases.proof: Standard-mandated iteration cost for unordered_map is O(size + bucket_count). bucket_count is influenced by the container's rehashing history (insertions, erasures, reserve calls) that this function has no visibility into, so it cannot be bounded purely in terms of the current element count n without additional implementation-specific assumptions.
cases.assumptions: Would be O(n) under the common assumption that bucket_count stays proportional to size (default max_load_factor with no unusual reserve/erase history), but that assumption is not guaranteed by the standard and is not verifiable from this function alone.

cases.proof: The outer array<vector<int>,4> always has exactly 4 buckets (a compile-time constant), so the outer loop contributes only a constant factor. The inner range-for visits every element of every bucket exactly once, giving total time proportional to n, the sum of all bucket sizes.
cases.assumptions: n = sum of buckets[i].size() over the 4 fixed buckets.

cases.proof: The loop visits each element of v once and vector::size() is O(1). Writing through an int* can change an element value but cannot mutate the vector object's size or loop bound in this function, so the work is O(n).
cases.assumptions: The supplied int pointer is valid whenever it is non-null; auxiliary space excludes the input vector and pointer.

cases.proof: std::array<int, N> has a fixed size known at compile time per instantiation, but from the analyzer's perspective N is a template parameter (an input symbol), not a fixed literal. Reverse iteration via rbegin()/rend() visits each of the N elements exactly once with O(1) per-step cost, giving O(n) time where n = N for a given instantiation.
cases.assumptions: n is treated as the template parameter N of the specific instantiation being analyzed, since N varies across call sites/instantiations.
